title: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence from begin to end, where each step changes exactly one letter and every intermediate word is in the dictionary, or zero if none exists.
shortTitle: Word Ladder: BFS changing one letter at a time
keyPoints: Model words as graph nodes with edges between words differing by exactly one letter
BFS from the begin word finds the shortest transformation sequence because it explores by distance
Generate neighbors by trying every single-letter substitution and checking dictionary membership
A HashSet for the dictionary gives O(1) membership checks, avoiding quadratic pair comparisons
Time is O(N * L * 26) where N is dictionary size and L is word length
Bidirectional BFS from both ends can dramatically reduce the search space on large dictionaries

s1_definition.oneliner: Treat words as nodes with edges between one-letter-apart words and BFS from begin; the level at which end is first reached is the shortest ladder length.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Word Ladder** models words as graph nodes connected by edges when they differ by exactly one letter.
- **BFS** from the begin word explores by distance, so the first arrival at the end word is the shortest transformation sequence.
- **Neighbor generation** tries every single-letter substitution at each position and keeps only dictionary words.
- **HashSet** for the dictionary enables O(1) membership checks, avoiding quadratic pair-wise comparison.
- **Time** is O(N * L * 26); **space** is O(N) for the dictionary and visited sets.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of transforming one account-status code into another at the National Bank of India by changing one character at a time, where every intermediate step must still be a valid code in the approved list. You explore all codes one change away, then all codes two changes away, in expanding waves. The first wave that reaches the target code tells you the fewest steps needed.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Ladder asks for the shortest transformation from a begin word to an end word, changing one letter per step with every intermediate word in a dictionary. The key insight is to model this as an implicit graph where words are nodes and edges connect one-letter-apart words, then run BFS because all edges have equal weight.

The efficiency comes from generating neighbors by single-letter substitution rather than comparing all pairs of words. For each word, try all 26 letters at each position and check the result against a HashSet, which is O(L * 26) per word instead of O(N * L) for pair comparison. BFS processes the queue level by level, and the first time it generates the end word, the current level plus one is the answer.

The senior point is bidirectional BFS: expand from both ends simultaneously, always choosing the smaller frontier, and stop when they meet. This reduces the search space from exponential in the distance to exponential in half the distance, which can be a dramatic speedup on large dictionaries.

At the National Bank of India, account-status codes had to migrate to a target code one character at a time through approved intermediate codes. BFS gave the shortest migration path, and the HashSet of approved codes made each membership check O(1).

Remember one sentence: model words as a graph, BFS gives the shortest ladder, and generate neighbors by substitution, not by comparing all pairs.
